issues.legal_issue: A High Court in a second appeal may not reappraise evidence and displace factual findings of the first appellate court without sufficient basis.
material_facts: The first appellate court analysed the evidence, accepted the testimony of the two attesting witnesses, and found the will proved.

The High Court re-assessed the evidence and reversed that finding, although the first appellate court had given cogent reasons for accepting the witnesses and had considered the alleged non-disclosure of the will.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not right to reappraise the evidence in second appeal and reject the will; the first appellate court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, findings of fact reached by the first appellate court are not disturbed in second appeal. The Court relied on the first appellate court’s reasoned assessment of the evidence and stated that it was difficult to justify the High Court’s reassessment in this case.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made in a second appeal.
predicates.reasoned_first_appellate_finding: The first appellate court made a factual finding after analysing the evidence and giving reasons for its assessment.
predicates.no_sufficient_basis_to_reopen_facts: The record disclosed no sufficient basis for the High Court to reassess and displace the first appellate court’s factual finding.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges a reasoned factual finding made by the first appellate court and there is no sufficient basis to reopen the facts, that finding must not be displaced.

issues.legal_issue: A will is proved where the evidence establishes its execution and attestation and the circumstances relied on to question it do not give rise to a sufficient suspicion about its genuineness.
material_facts: Two attesting witnesses testified that the testatrix signed the will in their presence and that they signed it in the presence of the testatrix and each other; the first appellate court accepted their evidence.
The will benefited a relative who had maintained good relations with and looked after the testatrix; the beneficiary and her husband were not present at the will’s execution.
The claimant did not specifically challenge the testatrix’s signature, allege forgery or undue influence, or otherwise plead that the will was invalid.
The beneficiary produced the will when she relied on it in her written statement; her earlier silence had occurred during proceedings focused on possession rather than title.
The first appellate court compared the testatrix’s signature on the will with undisputed signatures on rent receipts and found the signature genuine.
The testatrix was about fifty when she made the will, and the will itself referred to her physical weakness.
issues.conclusion: The alleged circumstances did not make the will suspicious; the will was proved, and the beneficiary’s title under it was established.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be proved like any other document, with proof of the testator’s testamentary capacity and signature required in the absence of suspicious circumstances. Where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. Circumstances identified as potentially suspicious include the propounder’s prominent role in execution coupled with substantial benefit, a shaky signature, a testator of feeble mind likely to be influenced, and an unfair or unjust disposition. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, and Guro v. Atma Singh. It also relied on Choteynarain Singh v. Mussamat Ratan Koer and Kristo Gopal Nath v. Baidya Nath for the principle that an asserted improbability must be clear and cogent, approaching impossibility, to prevail against a large and consistent body of evidence of execution and attestation. The testator’s age and the absence of an apparent motive, by themselves, did not make the will suspicious.

rule.if: will_dispute and attesting_witnesses_support_execution and signature_supported and natural_beneficiary_relationship and no_material_suspicious_circumstances

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim of title based on a will.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_support_execution: Attesting witnesses testified to the testator’s signing and the required attestation, and their evidence was accepted by the fact-finding court.
predicates.signature_supported: Evidence supported the genuineness of the testator’s signature on the will.
predicates.natural_beneficiary_relationship: The will benefited a person whose relationship and conduct toward the testator made the disposition natural in the circumstances.
predicates.no_material_suspicious_circumstances: The alleged concerns, including delayed disclosure or the testator’s age, did not establish a material suspicious circumstance, and no other material circumstance undermined the will.

issues.definition: In a will dispute, when accepted attesting testimony and supporting signature evidence establish execution, the beneficiary relationship makes the disposition natural, and no material suspicious circumstance remains, the will is proved.
